transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-04-09 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 78 minutes (scheduled)
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Rivera (Redwood SE), Sahil Mehta (Aurum Head of ML), Priya Kapoor (Aurum Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (Aurum SRE), Juno Lee (Aurum Eng Mgr)

Summary:
This was a technical deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail latency for streaming and non-streaming inference paths. Primary concerns: cross-region network hops, KV (K-V) cache hit patterns, batching windows, quantization impact on latency and variance, and VPC/on-prem TLS termination. Customer wants guidance for a pilot to get p99 < 200ms for streaming responses for short chat flows, and p95 < 90ms for token-level generation on dedicated pool.

Referenced artifacts:
- internal benchmark sheet: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/aurum-p99-2025 (shared)
- security & VPC checklist (slide deck) - will be shared after call

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: hey everybody, thanks for joining, um quick intros — Diego and I from Redwood — we'll do a short agenda: current numbers, root causes for tail, potential levers (kv, batching, q), and a proposed POC.
[00:00:18] Sahil: yeah thanks, we really want to get ahead of these spikes. For our payments chatflow 75% of requests are short (<= 40 tokens) streaming responses. p95 is okay but p99 spikes to 600-800ms and that's killing UX.
[00:00:37] Diego: ok that's helpful, thanks. quick clarifying q: those p99 numbers are client-observed or infra-instrumented?
[00:00:42] Sahil: client observed — we measured in front-end with trace ids, but we also have traces from our edge LB.
[00:00:50] Priya: and just to add, some of the p99s correlate with cross-region fallbacks — we failover to the eu-west region overnight for some traffic and that adds extra hops.
[00:01:03] Maya: great, so we should bracket network vs server-side tail. Diego, can you walk through where Redwood sees queuing and kernel scheduling?
[00:01:12] Diego: sure. big picture: tail latency comes from three main buckets — network (TLS handshakes, extra TCP hops), queueing inside the runtime (batch formation + head-of-line blocking), and GPU-side variance (kernel preemption, context switch, memory thrash). For streaming there is also framing + chunking overhead if the SDK does small writes.
[00:01:39] Sahil: when you say queueing inside runtime, is that the continuous batching window that's configurable?
[00:01:44] Diego: yes exactly. we have a batching window and also dynamic batching threshold. for small short requests, a longer micro-batching window will increase throughput but will push the p95/p99 up — because a request might wait up to the batch timeout. we saw in your sample traces a batch wait of ~25-30ms sometimes, then an additional 20-30ms at scheduling.
[00:02:06] Liam: there's also socket-level issues we've seen — client libs opening fresh conns due to aggressive dns / ephemeral ports. TLS overhead per-request is non-trivial at p99s.
[00:02:16] Diego: right. one mitigation is keepalives and connection pooling at the client. another is offloading TLS to an LB in the same VPC to reduce the handshake cost; but in private/on-prem you might want mTLS which costs you CPU cycles on the edge host.
[00:02:31] Juno: can you expand on KV cache? we assumed enabling KV cache would drastically reduce p99 for streaming but we saw mixed results.
[00:02:38] Diego: KV cache helps when you have repeated prefixes and stable sessions. in your chatflow you have a lot of similar prompts, but the problem was cache miss amplification: the KV shards had hot entries, and when a shard evicted entries you got sudden p99 spikes because lookups hit disk/page or had to fetch from slow path.
[00:02:59] Priya: is that our shards or the Redwood-managed shards?
[00:03:03] Diego: for the hosted run you saw, it's Redwood-managed. for Dedicated we can co-locate KV shards with compute to reduce inter-host hops. if you run on-prem the latency is typically lower but configuration-sensitive — you need enough RAM per shard and careful eviction policy.
[00:03:20] Sahil: ok so does co-location completely remove the p99 spike?
[00:03:24] Diego: it reduces the network variance side. but you still can have GPU-side queuing. however, co-located KV + prefix caching means many hits are in-memory and sub-ms. the p99 then becomes dominated by queueing and kernel preemption.
[00:03:38] Maya: quick interjection — we recorded some samples where p99 correlated with garbage collection and python worker restarts on our side. any guidance there?
[00:03:47] Diego: yes run as few python worker processes as possible for the low-latency path, or use our compiled runtime path which avoids python in the hot loop. also set up health probes and an aggressive restart policy for leaking processes.
[00:03:59] [00:04:00] Sahil: hmm noted. about quantization — we tried int8 quant for a smaller model and saw slightly worse p99 under load, that was surprising.
[00:04:09] Diego: quantization reduces compute but can increase kernel variance depending on kernel availability. if kernels are not fused or optimized on your GPU, quant can increase single-request latency and tail because the runtime falls back to slower code paths for some seq lengths. We recommend our quantization profiles — they'll pick kernels with stable tail characteristics.
[00:04:28] Priya: are you saying sometimes quant is worse for tail?
[00:04:31] Diego: yes, particularly for short sequences where overhead becomes a larger fraction. also mixed-precision kernels sometimes have higher p99 due to different memory access patterns.
[00:04:41] Juno: any specific GPU metrics to watch during a test?
[00:04:44] Diego: pcie bus saturation, kernel launch latency histogram, and GPU SM utilization variance. also watch CUDA context-switch counts. a steady 80-90% SM util is good, but large variance indicates batching misalignment.
[00:04:57] [00:05:00] Liam: networking again — can you quantify cross-region cost? we saw p99 jump ~120ms when traffic went to eu-west vs us-west.
[00:05:06] Diego: yes. each extra regional hop typically adds 50-120ms depending on route and LB. TLS term re-establishment if you don't reuse conn can add 100-200ms. For strict p99 targets it's best to route to local region or set a fallback policy that prefers local cold-capacity rather than remote warm nodes.
[00:05:22] Sahil: streaming vs non-streaming — the product team says streaming gives better UX, but does it increase p99?
[00:05:29] Diego: streaming adds framing overhead and more frequent writes, so if the network path has high serialization latency it can increase p99. But streaming reduces perceived latency because tokens arrive earlier. The real metric is end-to-end user-perceived latency; we should measure both first-byte latency and end-of-stream. In many setups, streaming improves median but can worsen p99 if the chunking is too fine-grained.
[00:05:50] Maya: practical config suggestions for Aurum's profile (short streaming chat):
- enable prefix KV cache co-located with compute
- use aggressive connection pooling at the client and keepalives
- set batching window to 3-5ms for short requests (trade off throughput)
- pre-warm a small dedicated pool to avoid GPU cold-starts
- apply Redwood's quant profile only after verifying kernel lat variance

[00:06:23] Priya: that 3-5ms window — does that mean we may need more GPU capacity to keep TPS?
[00:06:28] Diego: yes, moving to smaller windows reduces batching efficiency so you'll need more slots; but for short chat flows it's usually worth it to meet p99 SLOs. Redwood Optimize can recommend the slot counts based on your token distribution.
[00:06:41] Sahil: regarding cold-starts: we saw a spike when a pod recreated after an OOM, what are your suggestions?
[00:06:48] Diego: pre-warm using a small warm pool with reserved capacity (Dedicated). set memory limits conservatively to avoid OOM. use application-level circuit breakers so a sudden OOM doesn't route all traffic to fewer nodes. Also, our runtime supports fast model loading with checkpoint sharing which trims load time, but warm pool is the easiest fix.
[00:07:07] [00:07:15] Liam: what about tls offload — if we keep TLS at our LB and then use mTLS inside the VPC, is that best?
[00:07:20] Diego: yeah that's common: terminate TLS at edge for public traffic, mTLS inside for mutual auth. For on-prem you may prefer direct mTLS. Offload reduces CPU on host and sometimes reduces p99 by cutting handshake work on the critical path.
[00:07:33] Juno: curious about request fanout — we have some flows that call a reranker after generation, sequentially. does that create tail coupling?
[00:07:40] Diego: absolutely. sequential fanout multiplies p99 risk — if either stage has a p99 at 3x your budget, the overall p99 will blow past SLO. async patterns or pipelined reranking, or co-locating reranker in the same region/pool helps. Also consider reranking with embeddings once per session rather than per-message.
[00:07:58] Sahil: ok great. let's talk about measurement — what's the best tracing approach to separate network vs runtime tails?
[00:08:05] Diego: instrument at these points: client send timestamp, edge LB accept, runtime accept, batch dequeue, GPU kernel start, first token write, last token write. collect histograms for each stage and derive p95/p99. We can share a tracer config we've used—linked in the sheet.
[00:08:22] Maya: i'll add we have a small test harness (see bench link) that can replay your traffic shape and inject network latency to simulate cross-region. Diego can run a suite for your exact distribution.
[00:08:33] [00:08:45] Sahil: one last question on quantization: do you recommend post-training quant or QAT for tail stability?
[00:08:50] Diego: QAT tends to be more stable for latency because you can exercise the exact kernels in training and detect slow paths. but it's heavier. post-training quant is faster to test. for p99-sensitive workloads we recommend QAT plus kernel validation.
[00:09:06] Priya: any quick wins we can implement before the POC?
[00:09:09] Maya: yes — enable connection pooling, set batch timeout to 5ms, co-locate KV for hot prefixes (we can do a config change for the pilot), and pre-warm 2 N GPUs for an hour before business hours.
[00:09:24] Diego: i'll also run a targeted experiment: 1) streaming with 3ms window + prefix cache co-located, 2) streaming with 10ms window + remote kv, and compare p99 histograms. i'll attach raw traces.
[00:09:35] Sahil: that sounds good. also i'll get you the token distribution.
[00:09:39] [00:09:45] Maya: recapping next steps quickly: Diego will run bench and share results, Maya will send pricing and security docs, Sahil will share traffic shape, Priya will coordinate VPC details for the pilot, and we'll reconvene after Diego posts the bench results.
[00:09:59] Juno: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[00:10:03] Maya: thanks all — i'll follow up with calendar invite for the POC planning.
